 1                                      I.    INTRODUCTION

 2   Q.   PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

 3   A.   My name is Jonah B. Mauldin. My business address is the New Mexico Public Regulation

 4        Commission (“Commission”, “NMPRC”, or “PRC”), 1596 Pacheco St., Santa Fe, NM

 5        87505.

 6   Q.   WHAT IS YOUR POSITION WITH THE COMMISSION?

 7   A.   I am the Accounting Bureau Chief with the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission –

 8        Utility Division (“Staff”).

 9   Q.   WHAT IS YOUR EDUCATIONAL BACKGROUND?

10   A.   I received a B.S. in Mathematics and a Minor in Business Management from New Mexico

11        Tech University in 2020. I joined the PRC’s Utility Division as a Public Utilities Economist

12        within the Accounting Bureau in October 2021. Over the course of my tenure with the

13        Utility Division, I have completed over one hundred hours of public utility regulation

14        training courses, which include: NMSU Fundamentals of Rate Making, National

15        Regulatory Research Institute (“NRRI”) Introduction to Utility Accounting, National

16        Association of Regulatory Commissioners (“NARUC”) Rate School, Accounting Tools

17        Inc. Public Utility Accounting (CPE Course), Institute of Public Utilities (“IPU”)

18        Accounting and Ratemaking Course, as well as the Society of Depreciation Professionals

19        (“SDP”) Introduction to Depreciation and Depreciation Fundamentals Courses. I have also

20        attended several utility-focused professional conferences such as the NARUC

21        Subcommittee on Accounting and Finance and NMSU’s Annual Electric Utility

                                                    1
                                      NMPRC CASE NO. 25-00082-UT
                                   PREPARED DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                          JONAH B. MAULDIN
 1        Management Program (“EUMP") Advisory meeting. Prior to my employment with the

 2        PRC, I was employed as a Financial Systems Analyst with New Mexico Tech’s Budget &

 3        Analysis Department. My responsibilities included development of accounting reports,

 4        procurement of essential business data, creation of financial reports, allocation of budget

 5        throughout the University, updating and maintaining the resource planning software, as

 6        well as the University’s Chart of Accounts, and troubleshooting system wide issues.

 7   Q.   HAVE YOU PREVIOUSLY TESTIFIED BEFORE THIS COMMISSION?

 8   A.   Yes, please see Appendix A for a list of cases I have participated in.

 9   Q.   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY IN THIS CASE?

10   A.   My testimony addresses El Paso Electric Company's ("EPE") requests related to its

11        proposed revenue requirement, including cost-of-service adjustments and other ratemaking

12        proposals. My testimony evaluates whether EPE's proposed costs and regulatory treatments

13        are reasonable, supported, and consistent with Commission rules.

14   Q.   HAVE YOU INCLUDED ANY EXHIBITS IN YOUR TESTIMONY?

15   A.   Yes, I have included the following exhibits:

16        ▪   JBM-1 – Staff’s proposed jurisdictional revenue requirement.

17   Q.   HOW HAS THIS TESTIMONY BEEN ORGANIZED?

18   A.   My testimony is organized into sections that address specific components of EPE's

19        application and proposed revenue requirement. Each section evaluates EPE's proposals,

20        identifies any areas of concern, and presents Staff's recommendations, including any

21        necessary adjustments to ensure compliance with Commission rules and established

22        ratemaking principles.
                                                   2
                                      NMPRC CASE NO. 25-00082-UT
                                  PREPARED DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                            JONAH B. MAULDIN
 1   Q.   WHO ARE THE OTHER STAFF WITNESSES ADDRESSING MATTERS

 2        RELATED TO THE REVENUE REQUIREMENT PRESENTED IN THIS

 3        TESTIMONY?

 4   A.   My testimony presents Staff's recommended revenue requirement, which incorporates

 5        adjustments supported by other Staff witnesses. Staff witness Naomi Velasquez addresses

 6        disallowances related to the COVID-19 regulatory asset and EPE's Rate Case Expense

 7        regulatory asset, among other accounting topics. Matt Bandyk addresses capital structure

 8        and return on equity on behalf of Staff.


 9                                    II.     BACKGROUND

10   Q.   CAN YOU PROVIDE A BRIEF OVERVIEW OF EPE’S APPLICATION?

11   A.   Yes. On March 27, 2026, El Paso Electric Company ("EPE" or "Company") filed its initial

12        Application with the Commission requesting approval of revised New Mexico retail

13        electric service base rates. On July 17, 2026, the Hearing Examiner issued a Sua Sponte

14        Order vacating the procedural schedule and requiring EPE to file a single amended and

15        restated Application with a complete supporting filing package. EPE submitted its

16        Amended Application in response to that order on August 6, 2026.

17   Q.   WHAT TEST PERIODS DOES EPE USE IN THIS PROCEEDING?

18   A.   EPE's filing uses a twelve-month Base Period ending September 30, 2025, adjusted

19        pursuant to Rule 530 for the Historical Test Year Period. EPE's current base rates were last

20        authorized by the Commission in Case No. 20-00104-UT.

21   Q.   WHAT REVENUE INCREASE IS EPE REQUESTING?

                                                     3
                                           NMPRC CASE NO. 25-00082-UT
                                       PREPARED DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                               JONAH B. MAULDIN
 1   A.      In its original filing, EPE requested a revenue deficiency of approximately $70.6 million,

 2           or a 50.4 percent increase in base rate revenues. In the Amended Application, the

 3           Company’s revenue requirement increased by about $85,000 resulting in an amended

 4           deficiency of approximately $70.7 million.1 However, EPE is not seeking recovery of this

 5           minor increase because the change is immaterial and represents only about 0.04% of the

 6           originally filed revenue requirement, EPE is maintaining the originally noticed revenue

 7           deficiency of $70.6 million.2

 8   Q.      WHAT ARE THE PRIMARY DRIVERS OF EPE’S REQUESTED INCREASE?

 9   A.      EPE identifies significant capital investment and inflationary pressures as the primary

10           drivers. EPE reports an increase in Net Plant in Service of $274.4 million, which

11           contributes to the proposed rate base increase of $260.2 million.3


12   III.    SUMMARY OF THE RECOMMENDATIONS IN THIS TESTIMONY

13   Q.      WHAT IS STAFF'S RECOMMENDED REVENUE REQUIREMENT?

14   A.      Staff recommends a New Mexico retail revenue requirement resulting in a net base rate

15           deficiency of $56,151,852. This figure reflects Staff's adjustments to EPE's amended cost

16           of service, as described in this testimony and the testimony of Staff witness Naomi

17           Velasquez. Since EPE is not requesting recovery of the approximately $85,225 increase




     1
       Amended Filing Direct Testimony of George Novela, 14:1.
     2
       Id. 12:15-21.
     3
       Amended Filing Direct Testimony of James A. Schichtl, 15:16-21.

                                       NMPRC CASE NO. 25-00082-UT
                                   PREPARED DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                             JONAH B. MAULDIN
 1        associated with the Amended Application, as noted above, Staff removed that amount

 2        before applying its adjustments.

 3   Q.   PLEASE SUMMARIZE STAFF’S SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATIONS.

 4   A.   Staff's recommended revenue requirement and the adjustments supporting it are addressed

 5        in this testimony and the testimony of Staff witness Naomi Velasquez. Staff's specific

 6        recommendations are as follows:

 7           i.   Regulatory Asset Amortization — Three-Year Period. Staff recommends

 8                amortizing EPE's requested regulatory assets over a three-year period rather than

 9                EPE's proposed two-year period. EPE’s historic rate case cadence creates a risk of

10                over-recovery with a shorter amortization period, and affordability considerations

11                support a longer period.

12          ii.   Carrying Charge on EIM and TVRPP Regulatory Assets — Disallow. Staff

13                recommends the Commission deny EPE's requested carrying charge on the EIM

14                and TVRPP regulatory assets. The Commission did not authorize a carrying charge

15                for either item, and the deferred costs are O&M in nature; deferral does not

16                transform their character or entitle them to a return.

17         iii.   Buena Vista Capacity Cost Deferral — Deny Recovery. Staff recommends

18                removal of EPE's proposed deferral of Buena Vista capacity costs. The Commission

19                did not authorize an accounting order or regulatory asset for these costs, and EPE

20                controls the timing of its rate case filings. EPE could have sought recovery earlier

21                and should not benefit from self-imposed delay.


                                                    5
                                         NMPRC CASE NO. 25-00082-UT
                                     PREPARED DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                             JONAH B. MAULDIN
 1            iv.   Short Term Incentive Plan — Apply 60/40 Cost Sharing. Consistent with

 2                  Commission precedent in Case No. 22-00270-UT, Staff recommends a 60/40 split

 3                  of Short-Term Incentive Plan costs between ratepayers and the Company.4 The

 4                  Company should retain financial stake in incentive pay program outcomes.

 5            v.    Capacity Costs to Base Rates — Conditional Approval. Staff recommends

 6                  approval of Santa Teresa Project, Carne BESS, Buena Vista 1 BESS, and BV1

 7                  LTPPA. The capacity costs have been previously approved by the Commission and

 8                  are non-variable and have traditionally been recovered through base rates.5 Staff’s

 9                  recommendation is conditioned on each resource achieving commercial operation

10                  before the rates established in this case become effective.

11            vi.   AMS Transition to Base Rates — Approve. Staff recommends approval

12                  consistent with the stipulation in Case No. 21-00269-UT, including capital costs

13                  through September 30, 2025, inclusive of AFUDC, and O&M.

14           vii.   Legacy Meters Installed After January 1, 2020 — 10-Year Amortization. Staff

15                  recommends approval of recovery but recommends resetting the amortization

16                  period to ten years rather than incorporating these meters into the existing six-year

17                  schedule. A ten-year period better reflects the spirit of the Grid Modernization

18                  stipulation and reduces ratepayer impact.




     4
      NMPRC Case No. 22-00270-UT, Final Order, p.54, paragraph 114.
     5
      The Buena Vista projects were approved in NMPRC Case No. 19-00348-UT, while the Santa Theresa & Carne
     Projects were approved in NMPRC Case No. 25-00038-UT.

                                      NMPRC CASE NO. 25-00082-UT
                                   PREPARED DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                          JONAH B. MAULDIN
 1        viii.   Accounting Orders – Peak Time Rebate - Staff recommends denial of EPE's

 2                request for an accounting order to defer PTR Pilot Program administrative costs, as

 3                EPE has not demonstrated these costs meet the extraordinary circumstances

 4                standard and has not provided cost estimates sufficient to evaluate materiality.

 5                Time-of-Day – If the Commission requires opt-out TOD rates, Staff recommends

 6                the accounting order be approved with the conditions outlined in this testimony.


 7                           IV.     REVENUE REQUIREMENT

 8   Q.   WHAT       IS   EPE'S     REQUESTED          REVENUE         DEFICIENCY         IN    THIS

 9        PROCEEDING?

10   A.   EPE is requesting an amended net base rate revenue deficiency of $70,723,779 on a New

11        Mexico jurisdictional basis. This is derived from a New Mexico base revenue requirement

12        of $210,685,584.

13   Q.   WHAT IS STAFF’S RECOMMENDED REVENUE REQUIREMENT?




                                                   7
                                     NMPRC CASE NO. 25-00082-UT
                                  PREPARED DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                         JONAH B. MAULDIN
 1   A.   Staff recommends a New Mexico jurisdictional net base rate revenue deficiency of

 2        $56,151,852, which is $14,571,927 lower than EPE's requested deficiency of $70,723,779.

 3        The difference is driven by two primary factors: Staff's recommended overall weighted

 4        average cost of capital of 7.249%, compared to EPE's proposed 8.354%, which reduces

 5        return on rate base by approximately $10.8 million on a New Mexico basis, and Staff's

 6        operating expense adjustments totaling approximately $3.74 million on a New Mexico

 7        basis. The rate base itself is unchanged from EPE's amended filing. Staff's adjustments are

 8        detailed in Table JBM-1 below and are supported throughout this testimony and the

 9        testimony of Staff witnesses Naomi Velasquez and Matt Bandyk.




10

11   Q.   WHICH ADJUSTMENTS ARE ADDRESSED IN THIS TESTIMONY?




                                                   8
                                        NMPRC CASE NO. 25-00082-UT
                                  PREPARED DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                           JONAH B. MAULDIN
 1   A.   Section VI of this testimony addresses Staff's recommended amortization period for the

 2        EIM Regulatory Asset, Rate Case Remand, TVRPP, Rate Case Expense, and COVID-19

 3        Regulatory Asset, as well as Staff's recommended denial of carrying charges on the EIM

 4        and TVRPP deferrals specifically. The Buena Vista capacity deferral removal is addressed

 5        in Section V(B). The STIP 60/40 cost sharing adjustment is addressed in Section VII. The

 6        Legacy Meters amortization adjustment is addressed in Section VIII. The membership and

 7        dues adjustments, rate case expense disallowance, COVID-19 regulatory asset

 8        disallowance, and the Advertising Expense disallowance are addressed in the testimony of

 9        Staff witness Naomi Velasquez. The capital structure and ROE will be covered by Matt

10        Bandyk on behalf of Staff.

11   Q.   DOES STAFF HAVE ANY NOTES ON ANY OF THE ADJUSTMENTS?

12   A.   Yes. Staff did not remove the entire $461,268 in advertising expense as outlined in Staff

13        witness Naomi Velasquez’s testimony because EPE increased the amount of advertising

14        expense it sought for recovery in the Amended Application. That increase, along with other

15        changes in the amended filing, contributed to the $85,225 upward change in the revenue

16        requirement. Since Staff removed the $85,255 increase, to avoid removing the additional

17        advertising expense twice, Staff’s adjustment removes only the portion of advertising

18        expense that was included in the original filing. Nevertheless, Staff maintains, as explained

19        in the testimony of Staff witness Naomi Velasquez, that all advertising expenses should be

20        removed.

                                             NMPRC CASE NO. 25-00082-UT
                                          PREPARED DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                                JONAH B. MAULDIN

 1                            V.     Capacity Cost Additions to Base Rates

 2                               A. Santa Teresa Project Annual Capacity Costs

 3   Q.        WHAT IS EPE REQUESTING WITH RESPECT TO THE SANTA TERESA

 4             PROJECT IN THIS PROCEEDING?

 5   A.        EPE requests inclusion of the annual capacity costs associated with the 50 MW New

 6             Mexico-approved portion of the Santa Teresa Project ("STP") battery energy storage

 7             system in base rates. EPE proposes Test Year Period annual capacity charges of

 8             $7,770,000.6

 9   Q.        DOES STAFF SUPPORT EPE'S REQUEST?

10   A.        Yes. Staff supports inclusion of the STP annual capacity costs in base rates. Capacity costs

11             are fixed and non-variable in nature and have traditionally been recovered through base

12             rates rather than through a rider or tracker mechanism. Further, the Final Order in Case No.

13             25-00038-UT expressly directs that "[EPE] shall address the cost recovery mechanism used

14             for the STP in EPE's next general rate case."7 This proceeding is that general rate case.

15             Consistent with that directive, and given the Commission's own recognition in Case No.

16             25-00038-UT of the systemic concerns associated with continued reliance on RPS Cost

17             Riders as renewable costs grow, Staff supports transitioning STP capacity cost recovery to

18             base rates at this time.

19   Q.        DOES STAFF HAVE ANY CONCERNS REGARDING EPE'S STP REQUEST?



     6
         Amended Direct Testimony of Victor Martinez, 19:11-18.
     7
         NMPRC Case No. 25-00038-UT, Final Order, p. 19, Ordering Paragraph L.

 1   A.        No. The STP capacity costs are known and measurable, the contract price is established

 2             and Commission-approved, and the facility is anticipated to be in service prior to the

 3             effective date of new rates. Staff would note that if STP is not in service prior to rates

 4             taking effect in this case, the costs should not be included for recovery in this case.

 5             Furthermore, Staff's support is limited to the annual capacity costs associated with the New

 6             Mexico-approved 50 MW portion of the facility. Staff notes that EPE proposed to address

 7             STP energy costs in its upcoming REA Plan filing, which has since been filed by the

 8             Company in Case No. 26-0000093-UT, rather than in this proceeding, and Staff does not

 9             take a position on that treatment here.

10                     B. Carne Energy Storage, Buena Vista 1 BESS, and BV1 LTPPA

11   Q.        WHAT IS EPE REQUESTING WITH RESPECT TO THE CARNE AND BUENA

12             VISTA 1 FACILITIES?

13   A.        EPE requests inclusion in base rates of the annual capacity costs for three additional

14             resources: the Carne 65 MW BESS ($8,572,200 annually),8 the Buena Vista 1 50 MW

15             BESS ($3,276,000 total Company, $670,096 New Mexico jurisdictional), and the capacity

16             costs incurred under the Buena Vista 1 Long-Term Power Purchase Agreement since that

17             resource came online in July 2023.9

18   Q.        DOES STAFF SUPPORT THESE REQUESTS?

         Id. 18:1.

 1   A.      Staff supports inclusion of the Carne BESS and Buena Vista 1 BESS annual capacity costs

 2           in base rates for the same reasons stated above regarding the Santa Teresa Project, these

 3           are fixed, non-variable capacity costs appropriately recovered through base rates, and each

 4           resource was approved by the Commission through prior proceedings.10

 5   Q.      DOES STAFF SUPPORT EPE'S REQUEST TO RECOVER DEFERRED BUENA

 6           VISTA 1 CAPACITY COSTS?

 7   A.      No. EPE's filing includes $653,366 representing one year of amortization and carrying

 8           costs associated with a regulatory asset reflecting deferred Buena Vista 1 (“BV1”) capacity

 9           charges accumulated since the resource came online in July 2023.11 Staff does not support

10           recovery of this deferral.

11           The Commission did not authorize an accounting order or regulatory asset for these costs.

12           EPE controls the timing of its own rate case filings and could have sought recovery of these

13           costs earlier. The absence of a Commission-authorized deferral mechanism means these

14           costs were recorded at EPE's own election, and ratepayers should not bear the consequence

15           of EPE's decision to delay filing.

16           Moreover, allowing recovery of this deferral would result in ratepayers paying twice for

17           the same resource. In this proceeding, Staff supports inclusion of BV1's ongoing annual

18           capacity charges in base rates on a going-forward basis. If the Commission were to also

19           authorize recovery of the deferred historical capacity charges plus carrying costs,

 4             This is also not the first time EPE has sought this type of treatment for costs related to this

 8             rejected that argument. Staff's recommendation here is consistent with that precedent.12

 9             Staff recommends removal of the full $653,366 from the revenue requirement.


10                                   VI.     REGULATORY ASSETS

11   Q.        WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF THIS SECTION OF YOUR TESTIMONY?

12   A.        This section addresses Staff's recommended amortization period for five of EPE's

13             regulatory assets, the Western Energy Imbalance Market ("EIM") implementation costs,

14             the Final Order on Remand regulatory asset, the AMS Time Varying Rate Pilot Program

15             ("TVRPP") costs, rate case expenses, and the COVID-19 related regulatory asset as well

16             as Staff's recommendation to deny carrying charges on the EIM and TVRPP regulatory

17             assets. Staff witness Naomi Velasquez addresses Staff's recommended disallowances

18             related to the COVID-19 regulatory asset balance and EPE's Rate Case Expense regulatory

19             asset in her testimony.

                                          JONAH B. MAULDIN
 1   Q.   WHAT AMORTIZATION PERIOD DID EPE PROPOSE FOR THESE

 2        REGULATORY ASSETS?

 3   A.   EPE proposes to recover the EIM, Final Order on Remand, TVRPP, rate case expenses,

 4        and COVID-19 regulatory assets each over a two-year period.

 5   Q.   WHAT AMORTIZATION PERIOD DOES STAFF RECOMMEND?

 6   A.   Staff recommends a three-year amortization period for each of these regulatory assets.

 7   Q.   WHY DOES STAFF RECOMMEND A THREE-YEAR PERIOD RATHER THAN

 8        EPE'S PROPOSED TWO-YEAR PERIOD?

 9   A.   Staff's recommendation takes into account the amount of time that elapsed between EPE's

10        last rate case and the present proceeding. A longer amortization period reduces the risk of

11        over-recovery in the period between this rate case and EPE's next rate case filing if EPE

12        were to follow a similar filing cadence. Affordability is also a relevant factor supporting a

13        longer amortization period, as it spreads recovery of these costs over a longer period and

14        reduces the immediate rate impact on customers.

15   Q.   WHAT IS STAFF'S POSITION ON CARRYING CHARGES FOR THE EIM

16        REGULATORY ASSET?

17   A.   Staff recommends denial of EPE's requested carrying charge on the EIM regulatory asset.

18        The Commission did not authorize a carrying charge for these costs. The deferred EIM

19        implementation costs are O&M in nature, and costs of this nature do not earn a carrying

20        charge. Deferral of these costs into a regulatory asset does not change their underlying

21        character as O&M expense.


                                                   14
                                          NMPRC CASE NO. 25-00082-UT
                                   PREPARED DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                             JONAH B. MAULDIN
 1   Q.   WHAT IS STAFF'S POSITION ON CARRYING CHARGES FOR THE TVRPP

 2        REGULATORY ASSET?

 3   A.   Staff recommends denial of EPE's requested carrying charge on the TVRPP regulatory

 4        asset, for the same reasons stated above. The Commission did not authorize a carrying

 5        charge for these costs, the deferred TVRPP costs are O&M in nature, and deferral does not

 6        alter that characterization.

 7   Q.   WHAT IS STAFF'S RECOMMENDED TREATMENT OF EPE'S RATE CASE

 8        EXPENSES?

 9   A.   EPE requests recovery of $2,015,800 in rate case expenses over a two-year period. Staff

10        witness Velasquez recommends disallowance of 50% of the requested balance, reducing

11        the recoverable amount to $1,007,900, as discussed in her testimony. Applying Staff's

12        recommended three-year amortization period to that reduced balance results in annual

13        amortization expense of $335,967. The combined effect of these two adjustments reduces

14        the revenue requirement by $671,933 on a New Mexico jurisdictional basis relative to

15        EPE's request, reflecting both Staff witness Velasquez's disallowance and Staff's

16        recommended amortization period.

17   Q.   WHAT IS THE COMBINED REVENUE REQUIREMENT IMPACT OF STAFF'S

18        ADJUSTMENTS TO THE COVID-19 REGULATORY ASSET?

19   A.   EPE requested recovery of $4,075,560 over a two-year period, resulting in annual

20        amortization expense of $2,037,780. Staff witness Velasquez recommends a reduced

21        regulatory asset balance of $2,603,185, reflecting her disallowance of $1,472,375 as

22        discussed in her testimony. Applying Staff's recommended three-year amortization period
                                                     15

 1             to that reduced balance results in annual amortization expense of $867,728. The combined

 2             effect of these two adjustments reduces the revenue requirement by $1,170,052 on a New

 3             Mexico jurisdictional basis relative to EPE's request, reflecting both Staff witness

 4             Velasquez's disallowance and Staff's recommended amortization period.

 5   Q.        DOES STAFF RECOMMEND DENIAL OF CARRYING CHARGES ON THE

 6             FINAL ORDER ON REMAND OR COVID-19 REGULATORY ASSETS?

 7   A.        No. The Final Order on Remand regulatory asset includes a carrying charge that was

 8             expressly authorized in the 20-00104-UT Final Order,13 and Staff does not recommend

 9             disturbing that authorization. EPE's COVID-19 regulatory asset request does not include a

10             carrying charge component, so no carrying charge issue arises with respect to that

11             regulatory asset.14

12   Q.        WHAT       IS    THE     REVENUE        REQUIREMENT            IMPACT         OF   STAFF'S

13             RECOMMENDATIONS IN THIS SECTION?

14   A.        Staff's recommended adjustments to the EIM, Final Order on Remand, TVRPP, Rate Case

15             Expense, and COVID-19 regulatory assets are reflected in Table JBM-1 above and result

16             in a combined reduction to the revenue requirement of $ $2,110,843 on a New Mexico

17             jurisdictional basis.

 2   Q.        WHAT IS EPE REQUESTING WITH RESPECT TO SHORT-TERM INCENTIVE

 3             PLAN COSTS IN THIS PROCEEDING?

 4   A.        EPE requests recovery of the non-financially based portion of its Short-Term Incentive

 5             Plan ("STIP") costs through base rates, calculated as a three-year historical average of non-

 6             financial STIP payouts allocated to O&M expense using a three-year historical bonus

 7             expense ratio of 61.53 percent.15 EPE has excluded the financially-based portion of its STIP

 8             and its Long-Term Incentive Plan entirely, consistent with prior Commission orders.

 9   Q.        DOES STAFF SUPPORT EPE'S STIP REQUEST AS FILED?

10   A.        Not in full. Staff supports recovery of a portion of EPE's non-financial STIP costs but

11             recommends that recovery be limited to 60% of the requested amount, with the remaining

12             40% borne by the Company's shareholders.

13   Q.        WHAT IS THE BASIS FOR STAFF'S RECOMMENDED 60/40 COST SHARING?

14   A.        Staff's recommendation of 60/40 cost sharing arrangement is grounded in Commission

15             precedent established in Case No. 22-00270-UT, a PNM rate case in which Staff advanced

16             the same cost-sharing argument and the Commission adopted it. The core principle is that

17             incentive compensation programs are more effective, and more deserving of ratepayer

18             support, when the company itself retains financial stake in the program's success. If

19             ratepayers fund the entirety of a STIP, the company collects those amounts through rates

20             regardless of whether awards are actually paid out. The company bears no financial

 1           consequence if the program underperforms. A 60/40 sharing arrangement ensures the

 2           company has a genuine incentive to ensure the program achieves its stated operational

 3           objectives, which ultimately benefits ratepayers.

 4   Q.      IS EPE'S STIP STRUCTURALLY SIMILAR TO PNM'S GROUP INCENTIVE

 5           PLAN IN CASE NO. 22-00270-UT?

 6   A.      Yes. Like PNM's Group Incentive Plan, EPE's non-financial STIP is designed to motivate

 7           and reward employees for achieving operational metrics. EPE requests that ratepayers fund

 8           these costs through base rates. The same structural concern applies: without cost sharing,

 9           EPE collects STIP amounts through rates whether or not awards are distributed, with no

10           financial consequence to shareholders if the program fails to achieve its objectives. Cost

11           sharing ensures that the company is incentivized to ensure the program is effective.

 3   A.     Yes. The AMS Stipulation in Case No. 21-00269-UT which was approved by the

 4          Commission contemplated that the stipulation did not apply to legacy meter investment

 5          made after December 31, 2019.17 Therefore, EPE has proposed cost recovery in this

 6          proceeding. Staff supports recovery of EPE's reasonable investment in post-2019 legacy

 7          meters consistent with the spirit of the AMS stipulation.

 8   Q.     DOES STAFF AGREE WITH EPE'S PROPOSED AMORTIZATION PERIOD

 9          FOR POST-2019 LEGACY METERS?

10   A.     No. Staff recommends that the post-2019 legacy meters be amortized over a new ten-year

11          period rather than being folded into the six years remaining on the existing amortization

12          schedule. The AMS stipulation established a ten-year amortization period for legacy meters

13          as the appropriate recovery period for these stranded assets. Incorporating the post-2019

14          meters into a compressed six-year schedule that was designed for a different, earlier vintage

15          of plant results in accelerated recovery that is inconsistent with the spirit of the AMS

16          stipulation and places unnecessary upward pressure on rates. A fresh ten-year amortization

17          period for the post-2019 meters better reflects the intent of the parties to the AMS

18          stipulation, appropriately moderates the ratepayer impact, allows EPE to recover the costs,

19          and treats this distinct group of assets on their own terms.

12             ACCOUNTING ORDERS?

13   A.        Staff evaluates accounting order requests against four considerations drawn from Case No.

14             18-00261-UT.18 Those considerations are: (1) whether the amount is material; (2) whether

15             the event was unplanned; (3) whether the event was beyond management's control; and (4)

16             whether the problem is unusual, abnormal, and not likely to be repeated. Staff recognizes

17             that these four factors are not the exclusive basis upon which the Commission may grant

18             an accounting order, and that the Commission retains broader discretion in appropriate

19             circumstances. However, in the absence of compelling policy or equitable considerations

10   Q.        DOES STAFF BELIEVE EPE'S PTR ADMINISTRATIVE COST DEFERRAL

12   A.        No. The PTR Pilot Program is a voluntary program of EPE's own design and proposal. The

13             administrative costs associated with running the program are planned, within

14             management's control, and not unusual or abnormal. These costs are the ordinary and

16             the administrative costs of a voluntarily proposed pilot program satisfy the extraordinary

 2        cannot evaluate the materiality of the requested deferral without a cost estimate. The

 3        absence of this information is independently sufficient to deny the request. Staff cannot

 4        recommend that the Commission authorize deferral of an indeterminate amount of costs

 6   Q.   DOES STAFF HAVE ANY CONCERNS ABOUT THE NATURE OF PTR

 7        ADMINISTRATIVE COSTS AS A DEFERRAL ITEM?

 8   A.   Yes. PTR administrative costs are O&M in nature and are the type of ongoing operational

 9        expense that is appropriately recovered through base rates rather than through a regulatory

10        asset. The fact that the PTR program is structured as a pilot does not change the character

11        of the administrative costs associated with running it. The administrative costs of operating

12        the PTR Pilot Program should be known and estimable in advance, and EPE has not

13        explained why base rate recovery is insufficient. If the concern is that the pilot may

14        conclude before EPE's next rate case, the more appropriate solution is to size base rate

15        recovery to reflect actual expected costs or to align the pilot timeline with EPE's next rate

16        case filing, not to defer an indeterminate amount of O&M expense into a regulatory asset.

17        Creating a regulatory asset for costs that do not meet the extraordinary threshold, and for

18        which no cost estimate has been provided, is not consistent with the Commission's

19        established framework for accounting order treatment and is not in the public interest.

 3   Q.   IF THE COMMISSION ORDERS MANDATORY OPT-OUT TOD RATES,

 4        SHOULD IT ALSO APPROVE EPE'S REQUESTED ACCOUNTING ORDER FOR

 5        THE RESULTING REVENUE SHORTFALL?

 6   A.   Under that conditional scenario, yes, subject to the limitations discussed below. This

 7        request is distinguishable from EPE's PTR accounting order request. EPE itself does not

 8        recommend mandatory opt-out TOD rates and has proposed the TOD rate remain opt-in

 9        pending completion of its pilot program. If the Commission were to order mandatory opt-

10        out TOD rates, the resulting revenue effect would not be a planned or self-designed

11        program cost within management's control, but a consequence of a Commission-directed

12        rate design change. Customer load-shifting behavior in response to a first-time, mandatory

13        default rate structure is inherently difficult to forecast and is not the type of recurring

14        variance addressed through normal test-year ratemaking. On that basis, the shortfall would

15        satisfy the unplanned, beyond-management's-control, and unusual/not-likely-to-recur

16        factors more readily than the PTR request does.

17   Q.   SHOULD THE ACCOUNTING ORDER, IF APPROVED, BE SUBJECT TO ANY

18        LIMITATIONS?

19   A.   Yes. Staff recommends the following conditions:

20        i) Symmetry - The mechanism should track both under- and over-collections relative to

21           the Commission-approved revenue requirement, not shortfalls only. A one-way

22           mechanism shifts all forecasting risk to ratepayers.

 1        ii) Defined duration - Deferral should be limited to a defined initial period following

 2           implementation (e.g., through EPE's next general rate case), after which any persistent

 3           variance should be addressed through updated base rates rather than continued deferral.

 4        iii) Attribution methodology - EPE should be required to support any claimed shortfall

 5           with a defined, auditable methodology isolating the portion attributable to on-peak-to-

 6           off-peak load shifting, as distinct from other causes of revenue variance.

 7        iv) Materiality threshold - At the time EPE subsequently seeks recovery, the company

 8           should provide support demonstrating the deferred costs materiality.

10        ACCOUNTING ORDER REQUEST?

12        approval of an accounting order for the resulting revenue shortfall, subject to the symmetry,

13        duration, attribution, and materiality conditions described above. If the Commission does

14        not order mandatory opt-out TOD rates, EPE’s TOD accounting order request is moot.
